say: Welcome to Challenge Day! There is no new topic today. There are puzzles from every lesson, and the only question that matters is: how do you START?
Clever inquirers do not always know the answer straight away. They have a toolbox of starts, and they check and explain.
Mix-up relay: I read a card, a volunteer answers and invites the next volunteer. You may pass once.
Look at the four puzzle cards. Which one do you think will be the hardest? Write your guess in the corner of your whiteboard and we will see at the end.
Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks, and before you touch the objects. Silent thinking. I will show the clock. Then talk with your partner.
stuck: Stuck: "How could you start? Draw it, list it, make a table, work backwards, or guess and check?"
Backwards puzzle: "Write the steps going forwards first. Then undo the LAST step first."
Logic puzzle: "Find a clue that tells you something for sure. Put a cross where it cannot be."
If a pair wants more: make a puzzle card for the next pair.

say: “A number is doubled, then 7 is added, then divided by 3, and the answer is 5. I work backwards and undo the last step first: 5 × 3 = 15, then 15 − 7 = 8, then 8 ÷ 2 = 4. I check forwards: 4 × 2 = 8, 8 + 7 = 15, 15 ÷ 3 = 5.”

“A logic grid. Ravi does not play swimming. Siti plays neither football nor badminton, so Siti swims for sure. A tick means crosses in the rest of that row AND that column. Ben does not play football, so Ben badminton and Ravi football. I check every clue.”

“How many squares are in a 2 by 3 grid? If I count only the small ones I get 6, but there are bigger squares. I count by size: 1 by 1: 6. 2 by 2: 2. Total 8. Counting by size means I do not miss any.”

do: Ask: "How did you start? Is there another start that would work?"
Ask: "Did you check your answer against EVERY clue?"
Ask: "What would you try first if the numbers were much bigger?"
stuck: Hint 1: “Draw a bar or a table. Put what you know in it.”
Hint 2: “Which clue tells you something for sure? Start there.”
Hint 3: “Undo the last step first. Fractions: if half was spent, half is left.”

do: Ask: "How did you start? Is there another start that would work?"
Ask: "Did you check your answer against EVERY clue?"
Ask: "What would you try first if the numbers were much bigger?"
stuck: Hint 1: “Draw a bar or a table. Put what you know in it.”
Hint 2: “Which clue tells you something for sure? Start there.”
Hint 3: “Undo the last step first. Fractions: if half was spent, half is left.”

say: “Pick one puzzle and tell your partner in two sentences. You can say: I started by ____. I know it is right because ____. You may pass.”
“Which start do you think was the most useful today? When would you NOT use it?”
ask: “Pick one puzzle and tell your partner in two sentences. You can say: I started by ____. I know it is right because ____. You may pass.”

Open. Praise reasons, not just answers. Good answers say what the start does: a model shows how the parts relate, working backwards undoes steps in reverse, a logic grid keeps clues tidy, listing by size makes sure nothing is missed. Different starts can both work.

say: “Today you used a toolbox of starts and checked every clue. That is how problem solvers work, and it is the end of our Math Inquirers program.”
“Do the exit ticket on your own, then show me. Then it is certificate time!”

p5l10-title.note: Minutes 0 to 2 (opening, inside the 90-minute clock). Objective: Choose a way to start a puzzle (draw a model, list in order, make a table, work backwards, guess and check or suppose, use a logic grid), solve competition-style problems, check every answer against every clue, and explain why the chosen start works. Materials: puzzle cards for 4 stations (backwards, logic, counting, guess and check), mini whiteboards, scrap paper, a 3 by 4 grid drawn on paper, certificates, stamps. Online: each breakout pair gets one puzzle card on screen and reports back how they started; logic grids and models are shared on screen and annotated together; children hold their working up to the camera. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson; every lesson adds up to 90): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6.5 (one hold-up for both puzzles, no volunteer round, nobody is marked), warm-up 6.5 to 13 (one game round, four quick questions), explore 13 to 27.5 (pair work 6 minutes at most, then two questions together; a Go further what-if is on the explore slide for any pair that finishes), teaching 27.5 to 38 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 38 to 42, workbook page 1 42 to 55.5 (the questions without a star; after question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder), check together 55.5 to 58.5, short teaching before page 2 58.5 to 60.5, workbook page 2 60.5 to 68 (alone: start with the questions named at the top, then choose; starred parts are take-home; nobody has to finish), check together 68 to 71, talk time 71 to 76.5 (you may say pass; volunteers first; the first step of the Investigation is take-home), exit ticket 76.5 to 81, reflection 81 to 83.5 (pass is always OK), certificates and goodbye 83.5 to 87, and the buffer 87 to 90 (floating time: spend it first if you run late, never fill it on purpose). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child and have no clock time. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and never splits a pair unless both children agree. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." In this last lesson the closing slot is certificates (12 seconds each). In this last lesson the 88 to 90 slot is certificates.

p5l10-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6.5. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Show puzzle 1 and give about a minute; click to show the short answer later. Then show puzzle 2 and give about a minute. Open with one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, drawing or counting, so everyone can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. ONE hold-up for both puzzles: after puzzle 2, everyone shows their paper at the same moment (own paper shown only to you as you walk round; online, all hold paper to the camera together, or show it to you only, on camera). Then click through the two short answers and say each with one short reason. NO volunteer round here (volunteers come in the talk time). Never boards in front of the group, never read out answers with names, no tally, no ranking. Never record scores. Answers and what to listen for. Q1: Ali blue, Mei red, Ravi green. Ali can only wear blue. Mei is not green and blue is taken, so Mei wears red. Ravi has green.; Q2: $24. Work backwards: 6 × 2 = 12 before lunch, 12 × 2 = 24 before the book. A bar cut into 4 equal units, 1 unit = $6, also works. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES (about 4.5 minutes). Show the two puzzles one at a time. Say one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is one that any child can try with objects, drawing or counting, so everybody can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Answers are shown PRIVATELY, never on boards in front of the group. Face to face: children write on their own paper and show it only to you as you walk round. Online: everyone holds their paper up to the camera at the same moment, or shows it to you only, on camera. Do not read answers out with names, do not keep a tally, do not rank. Use ONE hold-up for both puzzles (after puzzle 2, everyone shows their paper at the same moment), then click through the answers and say each one with one short reason. There is NO volunteer round in the sneak-peek; volunteers come in the talk time. Never choose a child because you saw a wrong answer. Never record scores. Choosing a start: every child has the same neutral line on workbook page 1: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (The number is the last question on page 1 of this lesson.) Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never single out a child by name and never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless BOTH children agree. Any child may swap at any time.

p5l10-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 10. Mix-up relay: SIX cards from our earlier topics (angles and patterns are in the quick questions). Read a card and ask for a volunteer; that child answers and invites the next volunteer. A child may say pass once, or choose a green (quick) or orange (think-about-it) card. Keep a private list so every child gets a turn before anyone has a second; do not call on a child by name who has not volunteered. Click to reveal each answer in order. A wrong answer gets a friendly "try again", never a groan. Answers: 1) the 5 is in the hundred thousands place: 500 000. 2) 4/6 + 1/6 = 5/6. 3) 8 × 5 ÷ 2 = 20 cm². 4) 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 cm³. 5) $6 ÷ 4 = $1.50 each, × 10 = $15. 6) 10% is $8, so 20% is $16. Volunteers who have not yet answered go first. Ask "Which lesson does this remind you of?" for each card.

p5l10-warm2.note: Minutes 10 to 13. Whiteboards up together, then click. Answers: 1) 48 ÷ 4 = 12, × 3 = 36. 2) 6 ℓ in 2 min is 3 ℓ per minute; 45 ÷ 3 = 15 minutes. 3) 180° − 65° = 115°. 4) add 3: 17. Ask after 2: "Which start did you use: a table, a rate per minute, or something else?" If you are short of time, skip question 4.

p5l10-explore1.note: Minutes 13 to 27.5 (the whole explore; this slide 13 to 23.5). Each pair solves ONE of the 4 puzzle cards and teaches it (online: send one card per breakout room as an image; the second card is the Go further what-if). Pair work is at most 6 minutes. Card A: a number is doubled, 7 is added, the answer is divided by 3, giving 5; find the number. Card B: Ali, Ben and Mei have a cat, a dog and a fish; Ali has no dog; Ben has no cat and no dog. Card C: how many squares of all sizes are in a 2 by 2 grid? Card D: two numbers add to 20 and differ by 6. Predict first: which card is the hardest? Children write the answer and how they started. Anyone who wants more (open to every pair): solve a second card, or make a puzzle card for the next pair. PROTECTED THINK TIME: before the pairs touch anything, say "Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks" and show the clock; then pairs talk and start. PAIR WORK IS CAPPED AT 6 MINUTES: say "Pencils down" at minute 23.5 and bring the group back (the minutes before that include the 30 seconds of thinking, finding materials and, in lessons that use them, the move to and from breakout rooms). GO FURTHER (say it as soon as a pair has finished the task): any pair that finishes early may try the what-if question on the next slide. It is open to every pair, not a reward. Answer: 6. Work backwards: 7 × 2 = 14, 14 + 4 = 18, 18 ÷ 3 = 6. Check: 6 × 3 = 18, 18 − 4 = 14, 14 ÷ 2 = 7. Any new card is fine if its working backwards gives a whole number and it checks when run forwards.

p5l10-explore2.note: Minutes 23.5 to 27.5. Pencils down: gather the pairs, then take one card at a time. Answers: A) 4: work backwards, 5 × 3 = 15, 15 − 7 = 8, 8 ÷ 2 = 4; check forwards. B) Ben has the fish, Ali the cat, Mei the dog (Ben has no cat and no dog, so fish; Ali has no dog, so cat; Mei has the dog). C) 5 squares: 4 small and 1 big; most children first say 4. D) 13 and 7 (guess and check, or: take away the 6, share 14 into 7 and 7, give the 6 back to one). Write the starts on the board as children say them: "work backwards", "tick and cross grid", "count by size", "guess and check". Do NOT give a method before they have tried; the next slides name them. TWO questions together only (about a minute each), then move on. GO FURTHER what-if (open to every pair as soon as it has finished; nobody waits): 6. Work backwards: 7 × 2 = 14, 14 + 4 = 18, 18 ÷ 3 = 6. Check: 6 × 3 = 18, 18 − 4 = 14, 14 ÷ 2 = 7. Any new card is fine if its working backwards gives a whole number and it checks when run forwards.

p5l10-teach1.note: Minutes 27.5 to 29. Teach: the toolbox. "Today's puzzles mix everything. Clever inquirers do not know every answer straight away. They know how to START." Click each card and give one example from our lessons: model (fraction word problems, Lesson 3), working backwards (percentage and fractions of a remainder), logic grid (today), list in order (digit puzzles, Lesson 1), table (patterns, Lesson 9), guess and check or supposition (Lesson 9). Click the last box and read it together. The next slides show three starts in action.

p5l10-we1.note: Minutes 29 to 30.5. Worked example: working backwards with fractions. Ask first: "What do we know? Only the END." Draw the steps as a machine going forwards, then go back along the machine with the OPPOSITE of each step, starting at the end. Think-aloud: "Half of what was left is $13, so what was left is $26. Before the $10 lunch she had $36. Now the tricky bit: she spent a quarter, so $36 is three quarters. If 3 quarters is $36, 1 quarter is $12, and four quarters is $48." Always check by running forwards. Common mistake: taking 3/4 of $36 or adding 1/4 of 36. Worksheet Q2 uses the same idea with different numbers.

p5l10-try1.note: Minutes 30.5 to 32. Whiteboards, then click. a) 19 − 4 = 15, 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Check 5 × 3 + 4 = 19. b) 9 + 5 = 14, 14 is half, so 28. Check 28 ÷ 2 = 14, 14 − 5 = 9. (Two items only.)

p5l10-we2.note: Minutes 32 to 34. Worked example: a logic grid. Read the clues aloud and let children say where a cross goes before you click. Click 1 shows the crosses from the three clues and the first tick: Siti's row has two crosses, so only swimming is left. Click 2 (step 2): a tick means crosses in the rest of its column, so nobody else swims. Click 3 (step 3): Ben has crosses for swimming and football, so badminton; Ravi has the one left, football. Ask: "Could we have started with a different clue?" (Ben also gets a cross in football, but Siti is the one with two crosses at the start.) Finish with: check every clue against the answer. This is the method for worksheet Q1, which has four people.

p5l10-we3.note: Minutes 34 to 36. Worked example: a model. "Ali is 3 units because Ben has 2/3 of Ali (2 units), so Ali is split into 3 equal units. Ben has 2 of those units and an extra $6." Draw the bars on the board while children say what to draw. Click step 1: remove the extra before sharing equally. Step 2: 80 ÷ 5 = 16. Step 3: Ali 48 and Ben 38. Check both clues, not just the total. Common mistake: 86 ÷ 5 without taking away the $6 first (17.2, not a whole number: a sign something went wrong). Worksheet Q3 is the same kind with Mei and Ravi.

p5l10-key.note: Minutes 36 to 38. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Q2: working backwards in the wrong order or taking away instead of adding back. (2) Q1: guessing instead of using a clue that tells you something for sure; not crossing out the rest of the row and column after a tick. (3) Q3: dividing 115 by 7 without removing the extra $10 first. (4) Q4: counting only the 12 small squares. (5) Q5: stopping at the first suspect that fits one statement instead of counting the liars for each suspect. (6) Q6: adding the same number of years to only one person.

p5l10-break.note: Minutes 38 to 42. 4 minutes. Online: everyone stands on camera. Children draw a 3 by 3 grid in the air, then count squares by size and whisper the answer to a partner or type it in the chat on the way back (14: 9 small, 4 of size 2 by 2 and 1 of size 3 by 3). Drink of water.

p5l10-ws1.note: Minutes 42 to 55.5. Walk around. Ask "How did you start?" and "How do you know?" before giving any help. Q1 is the logic grid, a good first win: clue 2 and clue 4 together fix the roti prata. Q2: the story goes book (1/3), lunch, gift (half). Undo the gift first, then lunch, then the 1/3. Q3 (draw a model) is done in the page 2 time, so leave it for now. Everyone sees the same neutral line: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (Question 2 is the last question to do in class on page 1 of this lesson.) Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless BOTH children agree. Think harder is the next pages after the Investigation page in the workbook. IN CLASS NOW: Q1 and Q2; Q3 is done in the page 2 time. Parts marked with a star in the workbook are take-home: say so once ("the starred parts are for home") and do not wait for them.

p5l10-ws1ans.note: Minutes 55.5 to 58.5. One pair explains Q2, the heaviest; click through Q1 (Q3 is checked on the page 2 check slide). Click each answer after a pair explains how they started. Q2: 15 × 2 = 30 before the gift; 30 + 12 = 42 before lunch; 42 is 2/3 of the money so 1/3 = 21 and all of it is 63. Check 63 − 21 = 42, 42 − 12 = 30, 30 ÷ 2 = 15. Q1: roti prata is a girl (clue 2) and not Mei (clue 4), so Siti. Ali is not laksa or satay, so chicken rice. Ben is not satay, so laksa; Mei satay..

p5l10-teachsq.note: Minutes 58.5 to 60.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). Ask first: "How many squares?" Most children say 6. Click: the red square, then the teal square appear with step 2. Think-aloud: "I count by size, smallest first. 1 by 1: 6. Then 2 by 2: I slide the big square along: left or right, 2. 3 by 3 will not fit, so I stop." 6 + 2 = 8. The check slide for the next grid (2 by 4): size 1: 8; size 2: 3 positions; size 3: none; total 11.

p5l10-ws2.note: Minutes 60.5 to 68. Children work alone on Q3 (printed on page 1) and Q4 (a); Q4 (b) (c), Q5 and Q6 are take-home (starred). Q6b: look for children who can say WHY they chose a table or the age gap, not only which one. Page 2 is a menu, not a wall. Everyone sees the same line: start with Q3 (it is on page 1) and Q4 (a), then choose. Nobody has to finish; stop at minute 68 whatever has been done, because the check-together slide gives every answer with its explanation. Starred parts are take-home (their answers are on the check slide for you; do not spend class time on them). Walk round, ask "what could you try first?", and give the first hint before any answer.

p5l10-ws2ans.note: Minutes 68 to 71. One child explains Q3; click through the rest (Q4 (b) (c), Q5 and Q6 are take-home, their answers are here for you). Click after a child explains. Q3: Mei is 4 units; Ravi is 3 units and $10. 7 units + $10 = $115; 7 units = $105; 1 unit = $15. Mei 60, Ravi 55. Check 3/4 of 60 = 45, 45 + 10 = 55. Q4: size 1: 3 rows × 4 = 12; size 2: 2 rows × 3 positions = 6; size 3: 1 row × 2 positions = 2; total 20; no size 4 because the grid is only 3 rows tall. Q5: Ali did it: Ali lies (Ben did not), Ben lies (it was not Mei), Mei is true: 2 liars. Mei did it: Ali lies, Ben is true, Mei lies: 2 liars. Ben did it: Ali true, Ben lies, Mei true: 1 liar. So Ben. Q6: table: after 7 years Mum 48 and Mei 16. Or gap 32: Mei would be 16 (2 × 16 = 32), that is 7 years from now.

p5l10-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) $60. Work backwards: $24 is 2/3 of what was left, so that was $36; $36 is 3/5 of her money, so 1/5 is $12 and she started with $60. Check: 60 − 24 = 36, 36 − 12 = 24. A2) 15 numbers: 104, 113, 122, 131, 140, 203, 212, 221, 230, 302, 311, 320, 401, 410, 500. A3) 72 and 73 (145 is 1 more than twice 72). A4) Day 8. After 7 days and nights it is at 7 m. On day 8 it climbs 3 m to reach 10 m before it can slip.

p5l10-gofurther.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 45 litres, which is 3/8 of the tank. The 20 litres are 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6 of the tank, so the full tank holds 120 litres. Half full is 60 litres; letting out 1/4 of it (15 litres) leaves 45 litres, and 45 ÷ 120 = 3/8. B2) 3 fifty-cent coins, 6 ten-cent coins and 16 twenty-cent coins. Suppose all 25 coins were 20¢: that is $5.00. Every 50¢ coin comes with two 10¢ coins; this group of 3 coins is worth 70¢, and replacing three 20¢ coins (60¢) with it adds 10¢. The extra is 30¢, so there are 3 groups. Check: 150¢ + 60¢ + 320¢ = 530¢ and 3 + 6 + 16 = 25. B3) Siti, Mei, Ali, Ben. Mei is in chair 2 or 3. If Mei is in chair 3, the only chair not next to her is chair 1, but Ben is not on the left end, so that fails. So Mei is in chair 2, the only chair not next to her is chair 4, so Ben is in chair 4. Siti and Ali are in chairs 1 and 3 and Siti is on the left: Siti 1, Ali 3. Make up your own (printed under Go further): Make up a logic puzzle with three friends, three snacks and three clues. Swap and solve; does only one answer fit? Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l10-gofurther2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 45 litres, which is 3/8 of the tank. The 20 litres are 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6 of the tank, so the full tank holds 120 litres. Half full is 60 litres; letting out 1/4 of it (15 litres) leaves 45 litres, and 45 ÷ 120 = 3/8. B2) 3 fifty-cent coins, 6 ten-cent coins and 16 twenty-cent coins. Suppose all 25 coins were 20¢: that is $5.00. Every 50¢ coin comes with two 10¢ coins; this group of 3 coins is worth 70¢, and replacing three 20¢ coins (60¢) with it adds 10¢. The extra is 30¢, so there are 3 groups. Check: 150¢ + 60¢ + 320¢ = 530¢ and 3 + 6 + 16 = 25. B3) Siti, Mei, Ali, Ben. Mei is in chair 2 or 3. If Mei is in chair 3, the only chair not next to her is chair 1, but Ben is not on the left end, so that fails. So Mei is in chair 2, the only chair not next to her is chair 4, so Ben is in chair 4. Siti and Ali are in chairs 1 and 3 and Siti is on the left: Siti 1, Ali 3. Make up your own (printed under Go further): Make up a logic puzzle with three friends, three snacks and three clues. Swap and solve; does only one answer fit? Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l10-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then the "see it" slide, then the walk-through. The chairs puzzle (2) is Go further Q7; the rambutan puzzle (1) is in the question bank only. Answers: 1) 14 rambutans. 2) Siti, Mei, Ali, Ben.

p5l10-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answers. Ask: What do you know for sure about the pile at the end? Which chair can Mei be in? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p5l10-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. E1: eating half and 1 more means the pile after the day is half the pile minus 1. After day 3 it is 0, so the pile before was 2 (half is 1, 1 more is 2 eaten). Then 6, then 14. Check: 14: eats 7 + 1 = 8, 6 left; eats 3 + 1 = 4, 2 left; eats 1 + 1 = 2, 0 left. B3: Mei is in chair 2 or 3 (not an end). Chair 3 leaves only chair 1 free from her side, so Ben would be at the left end, which the last clue forbids. So Mei is in chair 2 and Ben in chair 4. Siti and Ali take chairs 1 and 3, with Siti on the left.

p5l10-talk.note: Minutes 71 to 76.5. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Good answers say what the start does: a model shows how the parts relate; working backwards undoes the steps in reverse order; a logic grid keeps the clues tidy; counting by size stops us missing any. Second question: "Which start do you think was the most useful today? When would you NOT use it?" Protected think time: before anyone speaks, everyone thinks silently for 30 seconds (show the clock). Then pairs talk. This applies to the explore, to the talk question and to any make-up-your-own prompt. The Investigation first step is take-home (or the opener of the next lesson): tell the group so at the end of the talk time. Talk-time rules: say "You may say pass." Ask for VOLUNTEERS first, then invite others only if they want to. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and no "who got it right?" hands. Talk time: 30 seconds of silent thinking, 2 minutes pairs talk, 1 and a half minutes volunteers share, then tell everyone that the first step of the Investigation (the page after workbook page 2) is take-home, or the opener of the next lesson. Pass is always allowed.

p5l10-exit.note: Minutes 76.5 to 81. Answer: $24. Work backwards: 7 + 5 = 12; 12 is half of his money, so 12 × 2 = 24. Check: 24 ÷ 2 = 12, 12 − 5 = 7. Extension: write your own logic puzzle with four people and four things. Does it have exactly ONE answer?

p5l10-reflect.note: Minutes 81 to 83.5. REFLECTION, about a minute and a half. Children use the small box at the bottom of the Investigation and reflection page: Something I did well; The hardest part was; What helped me (tick boxes include "I asked for help" and "I am still stuck (my tutor will check in with me)"). Pass is always OK. Never collected in public; you may read it privately later to plan the next lesson and check in with any child who ticked still stuck in the open session (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, parent nearby, never a private message). Never read a child's reflection aloud. It is never collected or shown in public. You may read it privately afterwards to plan the next lesson and to check in with any child who ticked "I am still stuck", in the open session (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby, never a private message). Never read a child's reflection aloud; only a child who volunteers may share. Praise strategy, not speed: "You tried a different way to start when the first one did not work. That is what we practised all holiday." This is the last lesson, so a volunteer may say what they would tell a friend starting the program. Then the certificates (see the next slide).

end.note: Minutes 83.5 to 87. Hand out certificates: show each one for about 12 seconds on camera and send the PDF through the approved channel. Ask each child to name one puzzle they enjoyed and one start they will use again. Give parents the one-page summary from the tutor guide.
